title: Opposition MPs say they want answers on planned Parks Canada cuts
summary: Opposition MPs are looking for answers about planned cuts to Parks Canada, with one saying Ottawa shouldn't proceed with its plan to continue free admission to parks through 2027.

image.caption: A Parks Canada logo is pictured in Banff, Alta., on May 15, 2025. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Opposition MPs are looking for answers about planned cuts to Parks Canada, with one saying Ottawa shouldn't proceed with its plan to continue free admission to parks through 2027.
Parks agency says up to 700 positions could be cut

Parks Canada sent a notice last month to some 3,000 employees stating it was planning layoffs. The agency has indicated upwards of 700 positions could be eliminated, along with Banff's dog search and rescue program.

In the latest federal budget, Ottawa said it plans to bring back the Canada Strong pass, which offers free admission to national parks, next year. Parks Canada saw a 13 per cent increase in visitors in the summer of 2025 after the special pass was introduced.
Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie said on Tuesday he's hoping to invite senior Parks Canada officials and union representatives to the House of Commons environment committee.

"Step 1 is knowing, right? Like right now, all we know is that half of the workforce on the ground got noticed as saying that your job might be cut," Leslie told reporters on Parliament Hill on Tuesday.

blocks.text: "There's nothing wrong with finding efficiencies in government. There is plenty of efficiency to be found. I will certainly have questions as to how top-heavy Parks Canada is."

Alberta Conservative MP William Stevenson, whose riding encompasses Jasper and Banff national parks, said if Ottawa is proceeding with the planned cuts, it should cancel the Canada Strong pass for 2027.

"I've got a lot of constituents, including Liberal supporters, that have written to me … saying they cannot accept having the Canada Strong Pass while they're also doing cuts. The two don't coincide," Stevenson said.

"But if they don't want to do that, they need to look at adjusting the program so that it actually works within the off-peak seasons. Have it operate now until the May long weekend. Don't add the problems to the peak seasons of travellers."
$24-million cut to agency this year
In a letter to Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, NDP MP Gord Johns said attracting more visitors to national parks with the Canada Strong Pass while also cutting staff "makes little sense."
"Employees have also raised concerns that Pacific Rim wardens could be required to assume enforcement responsibilities at Gulf Islands National Park Reserve," Johns wrote on Monday.
"While unconfirmed, this possibility raises serious questions about response times and adequate enforcement coverage at Pacific Rim."
Conservative MPs also took aim Tuesday at the amount of money Ottawa is sending to other countries, arguing that money could be spent to fund jobs within Parks Canada.
In its departmental report, Parks Canada forecasts cutting $24 million in spending this coming fiscal year, $45 million in 2027-2028 and $75 million in 2028-2029.
Castle Mountain in Banff National Park is shown in June 2023. (Colette Derworiz/The Canadian Presss)

"In that time we have money to go to China, to Brazil, $560 million no problem, Senegal for electric vehicles. Vietnam, Fiji, Peru, Mozambique — $40 million we've given," said Quebec Conservative MP Gabriel Hardy in French. He added that Parks Canada is not maintaining certain national monuments because of budget cuts.
The $560 million Hardy referred to was a pledge Prime Minister Mark Carney made earlier this month while travelling in Asia.
The money, spread out over four years, is slated to fund a joint initiative between Brazil and Norway to protect tropical forests and biodiversity, according to the Prime Minister's Office.
The goal is to protect more than one billion hectares of tropical forests annually across more than 70 countries.
"So on one hand, we're cutting the maintenance of the monuments under the care of Parks Canada. But we're giving our money everywhere else abroad," Hardy said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nick Murray is a reporter with The Canadian Press.
